event.title: HAI Seminar The AI 100
event.description:
AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI

Michael Wooldridge, Ashall Professor of the Foundations of Artificial Intelligence, University of Oxford

Moderated by: Russ Altman, Kenneth Fong Professor and Professor of Bioengineering, of Genetics, of Medicine, of Biomedical Data Science, Senior Fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI and Professor, by courtesy, of Computer Science

This talk will cover key insights from the third AI100 report, AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI, set for release in October 2026. The report was commissioned by the AI100 standing committee and led by study panel chair Michael Wooldridge.

Wooldridge will discuss how generative AI achieved World Wide Web-level impact in five years, largely unanticipated even by its developers; why software engineering became AI's first killer app and what that suggests for knowledge work; the unprecedented scale of AI infrastructure investment and the strains it creates; and the shift away from pure scaling toward reasoning and inference-time compute. He will also cover the concentration of frontier development among a small number of US and Chinese actors, expert disagreement over AGI timelines, and a governance landscape that remains fragmented.

The One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is a longitudinal effort administered out of Stanford HAI and managed by a standing committee of AI experts from around the world, chaired by Sheila McIlraith, Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto. Its mission is to assess AI not as a snapshot, but as an evolving force across technical, ethical, economic, and societal domains. Every five years, we return to the same standing questions and answer them anew in a changed world.

event.title: Make a Gutsy Move for Better Health
event.description:
The gut microbiome is a diverse colony of bacteria that resides in each of us. Emerging research shows these bacteria play a key role in a healthy immune system. They are also associated with conditions such as obesity, diabetes, irritable bowel syndrome, depression, and a variety of cancers. Yet most of us don’t know much about gut health or what to do to improve it.

In this noontime webinar, you will be introduced to this secret world inside each of us through evidence-based research related to gut health. You will learn how the microbiota within the gut function, including their role in health promotion and disease. We will discuss the difference between prebiotics and probiotics and identify sources in food and supplements. We will also address the role of nutrition in supporting the microbiome and the practical steps you can take now to support your gut health and improve your well-being.

This class will be recorded and a one-week link to the recording will be shared with all registered participants. 

To receive incentive points, attend at least 80% of the live session or listen to the entire recording within one week.

Request disability accommodations and access info.

Class details are subject to change.

event.title: The Greek and Arabic Reception of Ptolemy's Almagest between the 7th and 9th Centuries | Maria Mavroudi
tags: History of Science in the Arab World
event.description:
The period between the seventh and the ninth centuries has frequently been portrayed in scholarship as “dark”, especially because its intellectual production appears low. Overall, it is deemed as an empty interval between the end of the intellectual efflorescence of antiquity and the presumed renaissance of philosophy and the sciences in the Arab world enabled by the Greek-to-Arabic translation movement in ninth- and tenth-century Baghdad. This talk will re-examine these scholarly assessments by using the reception of Ptolemy’s Almagest as an example.

Maria Mavroudi was born in Thessaloniki, Greece and studied Philology at the University of her native city before earning a Ph.D. in Byzantine studies at Harvard. Her scholarly work begun by focusing on a tenth-century Byzantine book on dream interpretation that had been widely received in Latin and the European vernaculars and counted as the Christian dreambook of the Middle Ages. While generally viewed as a Byzantine invention partly based on the second-century manual of Artemidorus, she showed that it was a Christian adaptation of Arabic Islamic material and one among a larger group of texts originally written in Arabic or Persian and received into Greek between the ninth and the fifteenth centuries. During the next two decades, she worked on identifying the place of these translations within Byzantine literary culture and its reception in “East” and “West’ during the medieval and early modern period. This begs reconsidering the position of the ancient Greek classics within the Byzantine, Arabic, and Latin intellectual traditions, as well as the supposed marginality of Byzantium within a broader medieval intellectual universe.  Her work was recognized with a MacArthur fellowship in 2002. Mavroudi is Professor of Byzantine History at the University of California, Berkeley, with additional appointments at the departments of Ancient Greek and Roman Studies and Middle Eastern Languages and Cultures.

event.title: Truisms, Fiction and Women Writing: A lunch workshop with author Marie Darrieussecq
event.address: 450 Jane Stanford Way, Building 260, Stanford, CA 94305
event.description:
The French and Italian Department and French Speaking Worlds: Here and Now invite you to a lunch workshop entitled “Truisms, Fiction and Women’s writing” with acclaimed author Marie Darrieussecq. Darrieussecq is a French novelist, translator, and former psychoanalyst. She earned her doctorate in French literature in 1997 at the École Normale Supérieure. Her 1996 debut novel, Truismes (Pig Tales, trans. 1997), tells the story of a woman who slowly turns into a pig amidst a tense and depraved political climate. It became one of the best-selling novels in France and was heralded by critics as a provocative social satire and multi-layered tale of feminist emancipation. She has since published over 20 works spanning from novels, children’s books, essays and biographies. Her novel Il faut beaucoup aimer les hommes won the Prix Medicis in 2013 and her more recent works include Pas dormir (Sleepless, trans. 2021) and Fabriquer une femme (How to make a woman, trans. 2026). Darrieussecq’s rich oeuvre probes the unspoken boundaries of language and represents a fearless expression of the female body. All are welcome! 

RSVP for the lunch workshop here.

event.title: Slavic Languages and Literatures - A Ukrainian Century: Émigré Poets in Prague
event.description:
Please join us for the third Zoom of our series, dedicated to the interwar emigre poetry of Prague, where a fascinating group of Ukrainian poets and political activists camped out during the late 1920s and 1930s, featuring Amelia Glaser and Ainsley Morse, UCSD colleagues and translators of Vasyl Khmeliuk, Olena Teliha, Yevhen Malaniuk, and Natalia Livytska-Kholodna, who will read from their work and discuss the innovative poetics of the Prague scene. Convening the discussion will be Ostap Kin, co-editor of A Ukrainian Century: Poems, 1900–1999, an anthology forthcoming in Fall 2027 from World Poetry Books.

Register for A Ukrainian Century on Zoom

Co-sponsored by the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures at Stanford University and the Institute of Arts and Humanities, Russian, East European, and Eurasian Studies at UC San Diego.

event.title: Leonid Gozman — After Putin, After the War: Russia’s Next Chapter
event.description:
Neither Vladimir Putin nor the war in Ukraine will last forever. What political order is likely to follow, and what would it mean for Russia, Ukraine, and the West?

Leonid Gozman, a longtime Russian opposition politician and political psychologist, will examine the scenarios that may unfold. A Ukrainian defeat, he argues, would likely produce a new war almost immediately. The end of Putin’s rule poses its own risks, and the transition could prove more dangerous than the present. Yet Gozman contends that a post-Putin Russia would probably be better for its citizens and the international community, even if members of Putin’s circle remain in power.

That transition, he suggests, may open a narrow window for Russia to resume a path of normal political and economic development. This discussion will consider what such a path would require, what forces could close it, and what role domestic actors and Western governments might play in shaping the outcome.

The event will be moderated by Kathryn Stoner, Mosbacher Director of the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law and Satre Family Senior Fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies. Stanford affiliates are invited to attend in person, and all others may join online via Zoom; registration is required.

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Leonid Gozman is the former president of the Union of Right Forces and former co-chairman of the Right Cause Party (2008–2011). From 2008 to 2013, he served as director of humanitarian projects at RUSNANO, a state-owned enterprise that commercializes innovations in nanotechnology, and from 1999 to 2008, he was an executive board member and representative for governmental and NGO relations at Unified Energy System of Russia (RAO UES). An active participant in Russia’s democratic movement who has served as political advisor to Anatoly Chubais and Yegor Gaidar, he is also the author of eight books and is a lecturer at Moscow State University. He was previously a fellow at the Woodrow Wilson Center, a professor of psychology and Russian area studies at Dickinson College in Carlisle, Pennsylvania, and was a visiting fellow at the National Endowment for Democracy in Washington, DC.

event.title: Raising Well-Balanced Teens and Tweens
event.description:
Today’s teens face intense academic, social, and extracurricular demands. Even caring adults can unintentionally add pressure that contributes to stress, disengagement, or burnout. This workshop helps families reframe success, support balance, and strengthen connection with their tweens and teens. We’ll share research-based tools to reduce stress, encourage intrinsic motivation, and promote healthy development through adolescence.

Learning outcomes:

  • Explore data from Challenge Success-Stanford student and parent/caregiver surveys
  • Identify sources of unhealthy pressure and stress
  • Reframe success and foster intrinsic motivation
  • Strengthen teens’ resilience, engagement, and sense of purpose

event.title: Uncommon Knowledge: The Intellectual Odyssey of James Burnham
event.description:
In 1941, James Burnham published The Managerial Revolution, the book that made him famous. It introduced a theoretical framework that is enjoying a renaissance today among analysts across the political spectrum. Join us for a discussion of this pioneering work and James Burnham’s enduring influence on American politics.

James Burnham (1905–1987) was an influential postwar conservative intellectual. Educated at Princeton and Oxford, he became a philosophy professor at New York University and, in the 1930s, an active Trotskyist. His decisive break with Trotsky in 1940 set him on a new path: the following year he published The Managerial Revolution, a landmark of political theory. Burnham went on to serve as a U.S. intelligence officer during and after World War II. In 1955, he became a founding editor of National Review, with which he was affiliated for the rest of his life.

The Hoover Institution Library & Archives will present “James Burnham: Political Theorist / Conservative Influencer,” a pop-up display of items from the Burnham papers, available to view before and after the event.

event.title: Rethinking Holiday Treats: Enjoyment Without the Guilt
event.description:
The holidays often come with added pressure around food, especially desserts. In this interactive cooking demo, we’ll explore how to enjoy holiday treats without guilt or restriction while still honoring health goals. Participants will learn practical strategies for navigating desserts, incorporating fiber and balance, and building a healthier relationship with food - all while seeing simple, holiday-inspired treats made in real time.

Join us for this free webinar to connect with a supportive community, share experiences, and gain practical advice for achieving lasting diet and lifestyle changes. The Nourish to Flourish monthly webinar series, hosted by the Stanford Lifestyle and Weight Management Center, is open to all adults seeking to enhance their knowledge and tools for effective weight management and improved well-being. You don’t need to be a Stanford patient to participate—everyone is welcome!

This webinar will be presented by Gina Ringelstein, RD, CSOWM,  who is a registered dietitian nutritionist and board-certified specialist in obesity and weight management at the Stanford Lifestyle Weight Management Center.

event.title: The Disappearance of Enforced Disappearances in Kashmir: Militarization, Mourning, and the Production of Normalcy
event.description:
This event is co-sponsored by the Center for South Asia , the Abbasi Program in Islamic Studies , and the Department of Anthropology.

About the speaker
Ather Zia, PhD, is a political anthropologist, poet, short fiction writer, and columnist. She is a Professor of Anthropology and Gender Studies at the University of Northern Colorado, Greeley. She is the author of Resisting Disappearances: Military Occupation and Women’s Activism in Kashmir (University of Washington Press, 2019; Zubaan Books South Asia edition, 2020). She is the co-editor of Can You Hear Kashmiri Women Speak? (Women Unlimited, 2020), Resisting Occupation in Kashmir (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2018), and A Desolation Called Peace (HarperCollins, 2019). Her recent poetry collection In Kashmir: Writing Under Occupation was published by Agitate Collective. She is the founder-editor of Kashmir Lit, and co-founder of the Critical Kashmir Studies Collective. Ather is also a former co-editor of Cultural Anthropology (2022–2025) and Associate Editor of the Encyclopedia of Women & Islamic Cultures.

event.title: Three L.A.S.E.R. talks: Media Art, AI, The Self and Consciousness
event.location: The Hub at Stanford Research Park
event.location_name: The Hub at Stanford Research Park
event.description:
Please park at 3165 Porter Dr (free)

The LASERs (Leonardo Art Science Evening Rendezvous) are an international program of evening gatherings that bring artists and scientists together for informal presentations and conversation with an audience. This evening, chaired by cultural historian Piero Scaruffi, will feature these talks:

- Liat Berdugo (Media Artist) on "Technologies of the Surface: Embodying the Gestural Interfaces of Everyday Technology"

- Julia Markel on "Which self does AI remember?"

- Vinod Menon (Professor of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences) on "The Default Mode Network, the Self, and Consciousness in the Age of AI"

Liat Berdugo is a multidisciplinary artist and writer whose work investigates the relationship between technology, visuality, politics, and power. She is an Associate Professor of Art + Architecture at the University of San Francisco. Her work has been exhibited in the USA, Europe and Australia. Her book, The Weaponized Camera in the Middle East, was published in 2021. Along with Emily Martinez, she is one half of the art collective, Anxious to Make, and is the co-founder of the Living Room Light Exchange, a monthly new media art series.

Julia Markel is currently a final-year PhD student in Computer Science at Stanford, advised by James Landay. Her research interests are in human-computer interaction with a focus on human-centered AI. She is currently working on projects that span philosophy of the self and AI, specifically investigating how we can leverage the notion of the plural self to design AI systems and understand their effects on individuals' self-concepts.

Vinod Menon is Professor of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences, Professor of Neurology & Neurological Sciences and Education, and director of the Stanford Cognitive and Systems Neuroscience Laboratory. He and his team were among the first to discover that the human brain is organized into specialized and interacting networks of brain regions, which has resulted in a paradigm shift in how we investigate human brain function and cognition.

- Liat Berdugo (Media Artist) on "Technologies of the Surface: Embodying the Gestural Interfaces of Everyday Technology"

- Julia Markel on "Which self does AI remember?"

- Vinod Menon (Professor of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences) on "The Default Mode Network, the Self, and Consciousness in the Age of AI"

Liat Berdugo is a multidisciplinary artist and writer whose work investigates the relationship between technology, visuality, politics, and power. She is an Associate Professor of Art + Architecture at the University of San Francisco. Her work has been exhibited in the USA, Europe and Australia. Her book, The Weaponized Camera in the Middle East, was published in 2021. Along with Emily Martinez, she is one half of the art collective, Anxious to Make, and is the co-founder of the Living Room Light Exchange, a monthly new media art series.

Julia Markel is currently a final-year PhD student in Computer Science at Stanford, advised by James Landay. Her research interests are in human-computer interaction with a focus on human-centered AI. She is currently working on projects that span philosophy of the self and AI, specifically investigating how we can leverage the notion of the plural self to design AI systems and understand their effects on individuals' self-concepts.

Vinod Menon is Professor of Psychiatry & Behavioral Sciences, Professor of Neurology & Neurological Sciences and Education, and director of the Stanford Cognitive and Systems Neuroscience Laboratory. He and his team were among the first to discover that the human brain is organized into specialized and interacting networks of brain regions, which has resulted in a paradigm shift in how we investigate human brain function and cognition.

Detailed bios at:

The Stanford LASERs are co-sponsored by the deans of Humanities and Sciences, Engineering and Medicine, and by Chemical Engineering.

event.title: Reading with Martín Espada, part of the Lane Lecture Series
event.description:
The Creative Writing Program is pleased to announce the next event in the Lane Lecture Series: A Reading with Martín Espada.

This event is open to Stanford affiliates and the general public. Registration is encouraged but not required. Register here

____

Martín Espada has published more than twenty books as a poet, editor, essayist, and translator. His latest book of poems is called Jailbreak of Sparrows (2025). His previous book, Floaters, won the National Book Award for Poetry in 2021. He is the editor of What Saves Us: Poems of Empathy and Outrage in the Age of Trump (2019). Espada has received the Ruth Lilly Poetry Prize, the Shelley Memorial Award, the PEN/Revson Fellowship, a Letras Boricuas Fellowship, and a Guggenheim Fellowship. His book of essays and poems, Zapata’s Disciple (1998), was banned in Tucson as part of the Mexican-American Studies Program outlawed by the state of Arizona. A former tenant lawyer in Greater Boston, Espada is a professor of English at the University of Massachusetts-Amherst.
